prompt: A tall vertical sheet of old printed cartoon paper torn horizontally across its middle, the two pieces nudged back together so a ragged, fibrous rip zigzags from edge to edge, and through that rip shows a finger-wide strip of pale cream card, empty, reserved for a caption. Top piece, the year 1919: a wooden-slatted park bench with scrolled iron ends, inked in faded brown with a fine steel nib on grainy biscuit-toned stock; behind it a gravel walk, a low spiked railing, a gas lamp on a ribbed column, a bare elm, and far off a tiny lad pedalling a delivery bicycle. Nobody else on the bench; at its right-hand end slumps a portly tycoon, smooth-shaven, heavy jowls, a little pointed moustache, a polished silk top hat tipped forward over his right brow, a double-breasted frock coat tight across the belly, gold fob chain looped over the waistcoat, pale spats, a gloved hand capping a silver-headed walking stick stood between his knees, the other thumb tucked into a waistcoat pocket, eyes drooping with lazy self-satisfaction. Bottom piece, now: that exact bench from that exact viewpoint, inked by the same hand in sharp jet black on whiter stock, but its surroundings updated: a battered council bin, a thin modern street light with a flat LED head, square paving blocks, and a commuter in a hooded parka hurrying by, his face lit cold by the phone he stares at. On the right-hand end the tycoon sits again, an exact twin of the man above: jowls, moustache, hat tipped at precisely the same tilt, tight coat, fob chain, spats, stick, tucked thumb, drooping smug eyes, not one line older. Straight-on eye-level framing at sitting height, the bench drawn the same width in both pieces so its iron ends line up across the tear. One warm low sun from the left lights both centuries the same way, throwing long hatched shadows to the right; shading made of crosshatch and stipple, springy assured outlines, generous bare paper, the hand of a 1910s satirical magazine draughtsman. Every surface in the picture, sign, bin, phone screen and corner, stays bare of any marks: pure drawing. Thanks.
